steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The lighthouse had been automated for ten years before anyone remembered Elias was still living there.

He hadn’t minded the change. When the brass sent a letter saying the lantern would now turn itself, he’d simply folded the notice into a neat square and used it to level a wobbly chair. The light still swept the sea; ships still passed in the night. The work of watching remained.

Every evening, as the sky thinned from cobalt to ink, Elias climbed the spiral of stone steps. He knew each one by sound—the third from the bottom with its dull clack, the thirty-first with the faint echo that hinted at a hollow inside the wall. At the top, the glass room waited, smelling of salt and metal and old storms.

He checked the machinery out of habit, though the polished gears no longer needed his hand. When satisfied, he settled into the chair beneath the great lamp and took out his journal, a thick book bound in cracked blue leather. Each page held lines of neat handwriting: the date, the weather, the visibility of the horizon.

“Clear tonight,” he murmured, though no one was there to hear.

Beyond the glass, the sea moved like a single slow creature, breathing in the drag of the tide, breathing out in long white lines against the hidden rocks. The beam turned, steady as a pulse, tracing its path across black water. That light had been his first conversation every morning and his last every night for forty years.

On calm evenings, Elias imagined the ships as brief visitors to his island, their lights blinking in answer to his own. He liked to think captains looked up from their charts and muttered, “There she is,” when the lighthouse flare swept the sky. Knowing he existed in that unspoken gratitude was enough.

Storm nights were different. When the glass shuddered and the air turned to needles of rain, he felt every blast as a question aimed at the tower: Will you hold? Will you keep burning? Elias would stand then, fingers resting lightly on the rail, as if his touch might steady the stone. The beam cut through sheets of water, a bright blade, and he could almost hear it calling to unseen sailors: Here. Here. Here.

It had been a long time since he’d spoken to another person. Supply boats came twice a year, and the crew always seemed in a hurry. They shouted polite questions over their shoulders—“Anything you need, Mr. Elias?”—while loading crates of fuel and dry goods. He would nod, take the parcels, and answer in the same way every time.

“Just keep the visits coming.”

They were too busy to notice that his voice cracked a little on “visits.”

One autumn afternoon, when the wind had gone strangely quiet, a letter arrived. It came with the milk, the matches, and the sack of potatoes, tucked into the corner of a crate. On the envelope, his name looked unfamiliar, as if it belonged to someone he’d once met at sea.

The paper inside was crisp and official. The agency thanked him for his years of service and informed him, in precise language, that the lighthouse required no living attendant. Generators and sensors would do the rest. A boat would come in a week to bring him ashore. A comfortable room had been arranged, inland.

Elias read the letter three times. Then he folded it along the creases it already possessed, somehow unsurprised that the paper had known where it would bend.

That night, he climbed the stairs as always. The lamp turned, obedient to its program. He laid the letter beside the journal and looked out at the horizon, where the last smear of sunset lingered like something reluctant to leave.

“How do they intend to replace watching?” he asked the lamp softly. The lamp, of course, did not reply.

The days that followed moved like ships in fog—visible only when they were nearly gone. He packed slowly. A single trunk took care of his clothes and a few mementos: a brass compass with a cracked face, a length of rope knotted by his father’s hands, a small wooden carving of a gull. The journal would not fit, so he decided to carry it in his coat.

On his final night, the sea lay black and slick as oil. The air was so still he could hear the chuff of waves against distant rocks, a sound like someone breathing in sleep. Elias lit a small lantern of his own, more for company than illumination, and took one last walk around the circular gallery outside the lamp room.

He touched the stone as he went. Here was the place lightning had struck, leaving a faint spiderweb of cracks. Here was the pane replaced after a storm fifteen years ago. Here was the spot he had stood the night a fishing boat, engine dead, signaled with a dying torch—three pulses of desperate orange—until the lighthouse beam found it and a rescue trawler came pounding over the horizon.

That memory held him for a while. The way the fishing boat’s single light had flared, vanished, flared again. The way the waves had swallowed the sound of voices, leaving only the urgent flash, like a heartbeat running out of time.

He went back inside and sat at his desk. There was one more entry to write.

“October 3,” he began. “Visibility clear. Wind calm. Lantern automated and functioning. Keeper discharged from duty.”

The pen paused over the paper. Then, beneath the tidy report, he added a separate line, smaller and less certain of itself.

“Light remains.”

He left the journal open to dry and went to check the lamp one last time. Its gears whirred softly, indifferent to his presence. The beam moved on its path, sweeping water, rock, empty air, as it had for more years than he cared to count.

On impulse, Elias stepped into its turning arc and lifted his hand. The white rush of it washed over his skin, briefly warming the back of his fingers. He imagined the beam racing out to the dark line of the world where sea met sky, his small gesture traveling with it—a last, invisible wave.

When the boat came at dawn, he stood at the foot of the tower with his trunk beside him. The captain, a young man with salt-stiff hair, offered a hand.

“First time off in a while?” he asked.

Elias looked back up at the lighthouse. In daylight it was just a tall, pale structure on a ragged rock, its windows reflecting the morning. The lamp inside still turned, though its sweep was now faint in the sun.

“I’ve been away before,” Elias said. “I just never left.”

The captain didn’t quite understand, but he nodded anyway and helped him aboard.

As the boat pulled away, the island shrank, its details smoothing into a simple shape: a hump of land, a streak of grass, a column of stone. The lighthouse kept its vigil, the automatic lamp flashing its steady code.

Elias watched until the tower was just a thin mark against the sky, a raised finger pointing nowhere in particular. He wondered who would keep watch now—not over the machinery or the schedules, but over the simple fact of the light itself.

Then he realized: no one had ever watched him, either, yet he had stayed. Perhaps that was what a lighthouse truly was—something that chose to remain, whether or not anyone was looking.

When the tower finally vanished into the brightness, Elias opened his journal on his knees. The blank page after his last entry fluttered in the breeze. He took up his pen.

“October 4,” he wrote. “Sea calm. Land ahead. Light at my back, but not behind me.”

He paused, listening to the soft slap of water against the hull, the distant cry of unseen gulls. The morning sun was climbing, laying a silver path across the waves, bright as any lighthouse beam.

He smiled, just once, at the thought.

“New post,” he continued. “Keeper still on duty.”
